meta.title: Who really said "The most disrespected person in America is the black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the black woman. The most neglected person in America is the black woman"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Malcolm X said it, in Los Angeles on 5 May 1962 at the memorial for Ronald Stokes. The recording survives, and the popular version drops the next line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The most disrespected person in America is the black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the black woman. The most neglected person in America is the black woman'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Malcolm X — from his 1962 Los Angeles eulogy for Ronald Stokes, not a 'speech to women'. What the audio proves, and what quoters cut.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · Nation of Islam minister and human-rights activist
answer.sourceLine: He really said it, almost word for word. The lines come from the Los Angeles address circulated as Who Taught You to Hate Yourself?, delivered at the memorial service for Ronald Stokes — the Nation of Islam member shot dead by the LAPD on 27 April 1962. The audio recording survives ↗, and the three sentences run consecutively, exactly as quoted.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Who Taught You to Hate Yourself?
Memorial service for Ronald Stokes, shot by the LAPD on 27 April 1962
Archival audio recording, with circulating transcripts

source.excerpt: The most disrespected person in America is the black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the black woman. The most neglected person in America is the black woman. And as Muslims, the honorable Elijah Muhammad teaches us to respect our women and to protect our women.
trail: The UCLA Film & Television Archive ↗ sets the scene: LAPD officers raided Mosque No. 27 on 27 April 1962, killing Ronald Stokes; Malcolm X held a press conference on 4 May and, the next day, delivered a eulogy at Stokes’ memorial service before an estimated two thousand people.
The speech itself survives as audio, catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ under the title “WHO TAUGHT YOU TO HATE YOURSELF (May 5, 1962, Los Angeles)” and credited to Malcolm X.
A full transcript at Speakola ↗ carries the three sentences consecutively and verbatim. Its own dating of the speech — 22 May 1962 — differs from the recording’s catalogue date.

Notably, Wikiquote’s Malcolm X page ↗ does not list this line at all (checked 6 Aug 2026), and Quote Investigator ↗ has never investigated it — so the recording and its transcripts are the evidence that matters here.
source.excerptNote: In the circulating transcript ↗ this paragraph follows directly on the passage of rhetorical questions about hating the texture of one’s hair, the colour of one’s skin and the shape of one’s nose and lips. The fourth sentence is the one quoters almost always drop.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: Who was Malcolm X?
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · Nation of Islam minister and human-rights activist
author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha in 1925, he took the name Malcolm X as a minister of the Nation of Islam and became its most electrifying public voice before breaking with the organisation in 1964. He founded Los Angeles’ Temple No. 27 in 1957, which is why the killing of one of its members in 1962 brought him west and produced this speech. He was assassinated in New York on 21 February 1965, aged 39.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong details
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — this is one of the rare famous Malcolm X lines with surviving audio behind it. What travels badly is everything around the words: the date, the occasion, and the sentence that came next.

items.why: Widely repeated in music-press coverage of Beyoncé’s Lemonade sample, including Mic ↗ and the Speakola transcript ↗. The archived recording is catalogued as 5 May 1962, and the UCLA Film & Television Archive ↗ puts Malcolm X’s eulogy at the Stokes memorial service on that day. Both dates are still in circulation.

The framing is a modern one, used even in the transcript’s own title ↗. The address was a eulogy delivered to a general audience at a memorial service for a man killed by police; the passage about Black women is one movement inside a long speech about the raid.

A common variant swaps person for woman in the opening sentence — it appears in the headline and body text on Black Dawah Network ↗, with no source given. On the recording the parallel structure is “person… person… person” all three times.

The quote is almost never carried past its third sentence. In the speech Malcolm X continues straight into a credit to the Nation of Islam’s leader — that as Muslims they are taught to respect and protect their women. Whatever one makes of it, it is the frame he himself put on the words.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely his. He said them in Los Angeles in May 1962, standing over the coffin of a man the LAPD had shot — and you can still hear him say them ↗.

context.heading: Why it was said
lead: On 27 April 1962 roughly seventy LAPD officers descended on Nation of Islam Mosque No. 27 in South Central Los Angeles after two members were harassed on a false suspicion. Seven unarmed Muslims were shot. Ronald Stokes, a Korean War veteran and the temple’s secretary, was shot from behind with his hands raised ↗ and killed. William X Rogers was left paralysed for life.

Malcolm X — who had founded that temple in 1957 — flew to Los Angeles, held a press conference on 4 May, and the next day eulogised Stokes before a crowd estimated at two thousand. The famous lines about Black women are not a standalone aphorism: they arrive mid-speech, immediately after the “who taught you to hate” sequence, as the emotional hinge of an argument about who in America gets protected and who does not.
context.detailsSummary: What the speech is actually about
detailsBody: The bulk of the address is about the raid: the grand jury, the Los Angeles press, Mayor Sam Yorty, and a point-by-point account of how the shooting unfolded. Malcolm X calls the arrested men forward on stage and describes their wounds.

The Black-women passage sits inside a longer argument that police violence and internalised self-hatred are the same wound seen from two angles — which is why the “who taught you to hate the texture of your hair” questions run directly into it.
Historian Peniel E. Joseph ↗ treats the Stokes killing as the episode that galvanised Malcolm X against police brutality as a public cause.
context.pull: It is a eulogy for a man killed by police — not, as the internet usually frames it, a speech to women.
